**Summary of the Congressional Review Act (CRA) Report**

The Congressional Review Act (CRA), enacted in 1996, provides Congress with the authority to review and potentially overturn certain federal agency actions classified as "rules." The CRA allows Congress to use a joint resolution of disapproval to nullify rules that have not been submitted to Congress and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) for review. This process is distinct from the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which outlines notice-and-comment requirements for rulemaking.

Under the CRA, a "rule" is broadly defined, encompassing a wide range of agency actions, including guidance documents and statements of policy, provided they meet specific criteria. These criteria include being of general or particular applicability, having future effect, and being designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy. However, the CRA excludes certain actions, such as those related to agency management or personnel, or those that do not substantially affect the rights or obligations of non-agency parties.

The CRA's process requires agencies to submit rules to Congress and GAO before they can take effect. If an agency fails to submit a rule, it may not be subject to the CRA's disapproval procedures. However, in some cases, Congress has sought GAO's opinion to determine whether an agency action should have been submitted under the CRA. GAO has issued 21 such opinions, with 11 concluding that the action was a rule under the CRA and should have been submitted.

The CRA also provides for expedited procedures for considering resolutions of disapproval, including a limited time frame for debate and voting. The first time the CRA was used to overturn an agency action was in 2018, when a joint resolution of disapproval was signed into law, overturning a guidance document from the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection.

Overall, the CRA serves as a tool for Congress to review and potentially overturn agency actions, particularly those that may have significant economic or policy implications. However, the broad definition of "rule" and the lack of clear guidance on certain exceptions have led to some ambiguity in its application. GAO's role in interpreting the CRA and providing opinions on whether agency actions qualify as rules has been critical in facilitating congressional oversight. Despite these challenges, the CRA remains an important mechanism for ensuring transparency and accountability in federal agency rulemaking.
answers: The Congressional Review Act (CRA) allows Congress to review certain types of federal agency actions that fall under the statutory category of "rules." The CRA requires that agencies report their rules to Congress and provides special procedures under which Congress can consider legislation to overturn those rules. A joint resolution of disapproval will become effective once both houses of Congress pass a joint resolution and it is signed by the President, or if Congress overrides the President's veto. The CRA generally adopts a broad definition of the word "rule" from the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), defining a rule as "the whole or a part of an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or describing the organization, procedure, or practice requirements of an agency." The CRA, however, provides three exceptions to this broad definition: any rule of particular applicability, including a rule that approves or prescribes for the future rates, wages, prices, services, or allowances therefor, corporate or financial structures, reorganizations, mergers, or acquisitions thereof, or accounting practices or disclosures bearing on any of the foregoing; any rule relating to agency management or personnel; or any rule of agency organization, procedure, or practice that does not substantially affect the rights or obligations of non-agency parties. The class of rules the CRA covers is broader than the category of rules that are subject to the APA's notice-and-comment requirements. As such, some agency actions, such as guidance documents, that are not subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures may still be considered rules under the CRA and thus could be overturned using the CRA's procedures. The effect of Congress disapproving a rule that is not subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking may be subject to debate, given that such rules are generally viewed to lack any legal effect in the first place. Nonetheless, the CRA does encompass some such rules, as highlighted by the recent enactment of a CRA resolution overturning a bulletin from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau that was not subject to the notice-and-comment procedures. Even if an agency action falls under the CRA's definition of "rule," however, the expedited procedures for considering legislation to overturn the rule only become available when the agency submits the rule to Congress. In many cases in which agencies take actions that fall under the scope of a "rule" but have not gone through notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures, agencies fail to submit those rules. Thus, questions have arisen as to how Members can avail themselves of the CRA's special fast-track procedures if the agency has not submitted the action to Congress. To protect its prerogative to review agency rules under the CRA, Congress and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) have developed an ad hoc process in which Members can request that GAO provide a formal legal opinion on whether a particular agency action qualifies as a rule under the CRA. If GAO concludes that the action in question falls within the CRA's definition of "rule," Congress has treated the publication of the GAO opinion in the Congressional Record as constructive submission of the rule. In other words, an affirmative opinion from GAO can allow Congress to use the CRA procedures to consider legislation overturning an agency action despite the agency not submitting that action to Congress.

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) faces significant challenges in aligning its services and real property portfolio with the evolving needs of veterans. Key issues include geographic shifts in the veteran population, a transition from inpatient to outpatient care, an aging infrastructure, and limited stakeholder engagement. These factors contribute to underutilized and outdated facilities, which are costly and difficult to modernize. As of June 2017, the VA reported 430 vacant or underused buildings, many over 60 years old, and a substantial number of historic properties that complicate renovation or demolition efforts.

VAIP, which includes facility master plans, assumes all future growth will occur within VA facilities, despite the increasing use of non-VA providers for care. This assumption may not be accurate, and the process is costly and complex.

In response to these issues, the VA has taken some steps, such as discontinuing the development of VAIP facility master plans and planning to incorporate more flexible approaches. However, more comprehensive reforms are needed to improve stakeholder engagement, streamline planning, and ensure that facility alignment meets the needs of veterans.

The report also draws on the Department of Defense’s Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC) process as a model for VA. The report recommends that the VA adopt similar strategies, including setting clear objectives, developing transparent criteria, and involving stakeholders throughout the planning and implementation process.

Overall, the VA must address its infrastructure challenges and improve its planning processes to better serve veterans. This requires not only modernizing facilities but also enhancing communication, collaboration, and accountability across all levels of the organization. By learning from past experiences and adopting best practices, the VA can more effectively align its services and real property portfolio with the needs of the veteran population.

**Summary of the Report**

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has faced significant challenges in modernizing its financial management systems, particularly through the TRIO project, which aimed to migrate the financial systems of the Coast Guard, Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and Domestic Nuclear Detection Office (DNDO) to a shared services model. Since its creation in 2003, DHS has struggled with internal control and financial management deficiencies, which have hindered its ability to effectively manage operations and ensure sound financial practices. These issues led to the designation of DHS as a high-risk agency.

In an effort to address these deficiencies, DHS initiated the TRIO project, which involved evaluating and selecting a financial management solution. The project initially aimed to migrate the agencies to a modernized financial system provided by the federal Shared Service Provider, IBC. However, the process was marred by several shortcomings, including inadequate adherence to best practices in analyzing alternatives (AOA) and managing project risks.

The evaluation of the TRIO components’ AAs revealed that while DNDO’s process was relatively robust, Coast Guard and TSA’s AAs did not fully meet the four characteristics of a reliable, high-quality AOA process. These included being well-documented, comprehensive, unbiased, and credible. Additionally, DHS guidance did not fully incorporate several GAO-identified best practices for conducting AOA processes, which increased the risk of selecting an unsuitable solution.

The project also faced significant challenges in risk management. While some risk management practices were followed, others were not, leading to issues such as delayed implementation dates, increased costs, and difficulties in managing the transition. The lack of reliable cost and schedule information, along with poor communication and coordination, further complicated the project.

As a result of these challenges, the TRIO project experienced delays, increased costs, and a shift in strategy, including a decision to transition away from IBC and a two-year delay in the migration of Coast Guard and TSA to the new system. The report concludes with recommendations for DHS to improve its processes for analyzing alternatives and managing project risks, ensuring better alignment with best practices and enhancing the likelihood of successful outcomes in future modernization efforts.
answers: To help address long-standing financial management system deficiencies, DHS initiated its TRIO project, which has focused on migrating three of its components to a modernized financial management system provided by IBC, an OMB-designated, federal SSP. House Report Number 3128 included a provision for GAO to assess the risks of DHS using IBC in connection with its modernization efforts. This report examines (1) the extent to which DHS and the TRIO components followed best practices in analyzing alternatives, and the key factors, metrics, and processes used in their choice of a modernized financial management system; (2) the extent to which DHS managed the risks of using IBC for its TRIO project consistent with risk management best practices; and (3) the key factors and challenges that have impacted the TRIO project and DHS's plans for completing remaining key priorities. GAO interviewed key officials, reviewed relevant documents, and determined whether DHS followed best practices identified by GAO as necessary characteristics of a reliable, high-quality AOA process and other risk management best practices. The Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) TRIO project represents a key effort to address long-standing financial management system deficiencies. During 2012 and 2013, the TRIO components—U.S. Coast Guard (Coast Guard), Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and Domestic Nuclear Detection Office (DNDO)—each completed an alternatives analysis (AA) to determine a preferred alternative for modernizing its financial management system. GAO found that DNDO's AA substantially met the four characteristics—well-documented, comprehensive, unbiased, and credible—that GAO previously identified for a reliable, high-quality analysis of alternatives (AOA) process. However, Coast Guard's and TSA's AAs did not fully or substantially meet three of these characteristics, and DHS guidance for conducting AAs did not substantially incorporate certain best practices, such as identifying significant risks and mitigation strategies and performing an independent review to help validate the AOA process. Based on these analyses and other factors, the TRIO components determined that migrating to a federal shared service provider (SSP) represented the best alternative, and in 2014, DHS selected the Department of the Interior's Interior Business Center (IBC) as the federal SSP for the project. However, because Coast Guard's and TSA's AAs did not fully or substantially reflect all of the characteristics noted above, they are at increased risk that the alternative selected may not achieve mission needs. DHS also did not fully follow best practices for managing project risks related to its use of IBC on the TRIO project. Specifically, DHS followed three of seven risk management best practices, such as determining risk sources and categories and establishing a risk management strategy. However, it did not fully follow four best practices for defining risk parameters, identifying risks, developing risk mitigation plans, and implementing these plans largely because its guidance did not sufficiently address these best practices. For example, although DHS created joint teams with IBC and provided additional resources to IBC to help address risk mitigation concerns, it did not always develop sufficiently detailed risk mitigation plans that also included contingency plans for selected critical risks. As a result, although IBC's capacity and experience for migrating large agencies the size of Coast Guard and TSA was identified as a risk in July 2014, a contingency plan working group to address this concern was not established until January 2017. By not fully following risk management best practices, DHS is at increased risk that potential problems may not be identified or properly mitigated. DHS, IBC, Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and other federal oversight agencies identified various challenges that have impacted the TRIO project and contributed to a 2-year delay in the implementation of Coast Guard's and TSA's modernized solutions. These challenges include the lack of sufficient resources, aggressive schedule, complex requirements, increased costs, and project management and communication concerns. FATCA, enacted in 2010, is a significant U.S. law designed to combat tax evasion by requiring foreign financial institutions (FFIs) to report information about U.S. account holders to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). This reporting is done either directly to the IRS or through a participating country’s tax authority, depending on the intergovernmental agreement (IGA) in place.

The report outlines the key components of FATCA, including the requirement for FFIs to report detailed information about U.S. persons’ accounts annually on IRS Form 8966. It also highlights the complementary role of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and the requirement for U.S. persons to file Form 8938 to report foreign financial assets exceeding certain thresholds. These forms are essential tools for the IRS to track and enforce compliance with U.S. tax laws on foreign assets.

However, the report identifies several challenges in the implementation of FATCA. One major issue is the difficulty in matching data between FFIs and individual taxpayers due to incomplete or incorrect Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TINs). This has led to inefficiencies in the IRS’s ability to cross-reference and verify information, which is critical for identifying noncompliance and ensuring accurate tax reporting.

The report also discusses the impact of FATCA on U.S. persons living abroad, including increased compliance burdens, potential discrimination in access to financial services, and the risk of renouncing U.S. citizenship. These effects have been exacerbated by the complexity of the reporting requirements and the lack of clear guidance for taxpayers.

In response to these challenges, the report recommends several actions. These include the development of a comprehensive strategy by the IRS to leverage FATCA data for compliance enforcement, the improvement of data collection and management systems, and the establishment of formal interagency collaboration to address the issues faced by U.S. persons living abroad.

Overall, the report emphasizes the need for continued improvements in the implementation of FATCA to ensure that it effectively combats tax evasion while minimizing the burdens on U.S. taxpayers and financial institutions. It also highlights the importance of interagency cooperation and the need for legislative and regulatory changes to address the complexities and challenges associated with the reporting requirements.

Data quality and management issues have limited the effectiveness of the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) efforts to improve taxpayer compliance using foreign financial asset data collected under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA). Specifically, IRS has had difficulties matching the information reported by foreign financial institutions (FFI) with U.S. taxpayers' tax filings due to missing or inaccurate Taxpayer Identification Numbers provided by FFIs. Further, IRS lacks access to consistent and complete data on foreign financial assets and other data reported in tax filings by U.S. persons, in part, because some IRS databases do not store foreign asset data reported from paper filings. The overlapping requirements increase the compliance burden on U.S. persons and add complexity that can create confusion, potentially resulting in inaccurate or unnecessary reporting. Since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the U.S. government has appropriated approximately $2 trillion in discretionary budget authority for war-related and international emergency or contingency-designated funding. This includes $1.8 trillion for the Department of Defense (DOD), $154 billion for the Department of State and U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and $3 billion for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Coast Guard. The use of OCO/GWOT funding has evolved significantly since 2001. Initially, these funds were used to address unforeseen needs, such as the costs of military operations in Afghanistan and Iraq. Over time, however, the designation has expanded to include a wide range of activities, some of which are not directly related to war or defense. For example, OCO funds have been used for infrastructure, support operations, and even non-war-related programs like disaster relief and counterterrorism initiatives in regions not directly linked to active conflicts.

The Budget Control Act (BCA) of 2011 established spending caps for defense and non-defense discretionary spending, with certain exceptions for OCO/GWOT funding. This has allowed Congress and the administration to avoid sequestration by designating certain costs as OCO. However, critics argue that this practice has led to the misuse of OCO funds for base budget requirements, effectively creating a "slush fund" that allows for increased spending without triggering the BCA's spending limits.

The Department of Defense (DOD) has reported that OCO funding has not decreased in proportion to the reduction in U.S. troop levels in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria. This is attributed to the fixed costs associated with maintaining military infrastructure and support operations. DOD has also noted that a significant portion of OCO funding is used for activities unrelated to direct combat, such as the European Deterrence Initiative and other deterrence and counterterrorism programs.

This figure amounts to approximately 9.4% of total discretionary spending during this period. Congress has used supplemental appropriation acts or designated funding for emergency requirements or OCO/GWOT—or both—in statute. These funds are not subject to limits on discretionary spending in congressional budget resolutions or to the statutory discretionary spending limits established by the Budget Control Act of 2011 (BCA; P.L. 112-125). The Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985 (BBEDCA; P.L. 99-177) allows emergency funding to be excluded from budget control limits. The BCA added the OCO/GWOT designation to the BBEDCA exemption, thereby providing Congress and the President with an alternate way to exclude funding from the BCA spending limits. While there is no overall statutory limit on the amount of emergency or OCO/GWOT spending, both Congress and the President have fundamental roles in determining how much of the spending to provide each fiscal year. Congress must designate any such funding in statute on an account-by-account basis. The President is also required to designate it as such after it is appropriated to be available for expenditure. Debate over what should constitute OCO/GWOT or emergency activities and expenses has shifted over time, reflecting differing viewpoints about the extent, nature, and duration of U.S. military operations in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere. Some defense officials and policymakers argue OCO funding allows for flexible response to contingencies, and provides a "safety valve" to the spending caps and threat of sequestration—the automatic cancellation of budget authority largely through across-the-board reductions of nonexempt programs and activities—under the BCA. Critics, however, have described OCO/GWOT as a loophole or "gimmick"—morphing from an account for replacing combat losses of equipment, resupplying expended munitions, and transporting troops through war zones, to a "slush fund" for activities unrelated to contingency operations. Congress appropriated approximately $103 billion for OCO in FY2017 (8.5% of all discretionary appropriations), $78 billion for OCO in FY2018 (5.5% of all discretionary appropriations), and $68.8 billion for OCO so far in FY2019. Congress's decisions on OCO/GWOT designations will affect how much agency funding is available for military operations and foreign affairs activities overseas, how much is subject to the BCA caps, and how much is incorporated into regular budgets and long-term budget projections.

The report provides an overview of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), focusing on its political history, ongoing security challenges, and the impact of conflict minerals on global industries. The DRC, a vast and mineral-rich nation with a population of about 83 million, has experienced decades of political instability and armed conflict since gaining independence from Belgium in 1960. The most severe conflict, known as "Africa’s World War," occurred between 1998 and 2003, resulting in an estimated 5 million deaths. The eastern region of the DRC continues to face violence, with illegal armed groups and some members of the national military perpetrating attacks, including widespread sexual violence against civilians.

The DRC is a major source of four conflict minerals—tin, tungsten, tantalum, and gold—which are used in a wide range of products, from electronics to automotive parts. In response to concerns about the human rights abuses linked to these minerals, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) implemented a disclosure rule under the Dodd-Frank Act in 2012. This rule requires companies to disclose the origin of conflict minerals and conduct due diligence to ensure they are not financing armed groups.

In 2017, the SEC reviewed conflict minerals disclosures from 1,165 companies and found that most had conducted country-of-origin inquiries and performed due diligence. However, challenges in tracing the minerals’ origins persisted, with many companies unable to definitively confirm the source. While some companies claimed their products were “DRC conflict free,” only a small number obtained independent audits to verify this claim.

The report also highlights the ongoing issue of sexual violence in the DRC, particularly in the east, where armed groups and state forces have been responsible for numerous attacks. In 2017, the U.N. documented over 200 cases of sexual violence, and case files indicated a continued pattern of abuse. The report notes that political instability and the complexity of the conflict have contributed to the persistence of these human rights violations.

Overall, the report underscores the challenges in addressing the root causes of conflict in the DRC, including the need for greater transparency in mineral supply chains and stronger efforts to combat sexual violence. It also emphasizes the importance of continued corporate due diligence and international cooperation in promoting peace and human rights in the region.

The report provides an in-depth analysis of the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) current methods for collecting and reporting broadband data, with a specific focus on tribal lands in the United States. It highlights the challenges and limitations in accurately measuring broadband access for Native American communities, which are often overlooked or misrepresented in FCC data.

The FCC uses Form 477, a data collection tool, to gather information on broadband availability from providers. This form is used to create maps and reports that depict broadband access across the country, including tribal lands. However, the report finds that the current system overstates broadband access on tribal lands due to several factors. For example, the FCC defines broadband availability at the census block level, which can lead to entire blocks being counted as served even if only a single location has service. Additionally, the lack of standardized methods for determining coverage areas and the absence of data on affordability, service quality, and service denials contribute to inaccuracies.

The report highlights that these inaccuracies have real-world consequences. Tribal stakeholders and providers have expressed concerns that the overstatement of broadband access can affect the ability of tribes to secure federal funding for broadband infrastructure. Moreover, the lack of a formal process for tribes to provide input on the accuracy of FCC data limits the ability of tribal governments to ensure that their communities are properly represented in broadband maps and reports.

The report also notes that while FCC has taken some steps to address these issues, such as conducting a one-time special data collection for the Mobility Fund Phase II program, it has not yet implemented a comprehensive solution. The report recommends that FCC develop a more granular data collection process, establish a formal mechanism for tribal input, and improve the accuracy of broadband data to better reflect the actual broadband access on tribal lands.

In conclusion, the report underscores the importance of accurate and complete broadband data for tribal lands to ensure that federal funding and policy efforts are effectively targeting the most underserved areas. It calls for FCC to take action to improve data collection and engagement with tribal stakeholders to better serve the needs of Native American communities.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) collects data on broadband availability from providers, but these data do not accurately or completely capture broadband access on tribal lands. However, FCC considers broadband to be “available” for an entire census block if the provider could serve at least one location in the census block. This report examines the regulatory landscape affecting community banks and credit unions in the United States, focusing on the challenges they face in complying with federal regulations and the efforts by financial regulators to reduce these burdens. Community banks are generally defined as smaller institutions that serve local communities, often with management and board members residing in the area. While there is no universally accepted definition, many regulators and industry groups use asset size as a key criterion, typically considering banks with assets under $10 billion as community banks.

The report highlights that community banks and credit unions play a vital role in providing essential financial services, particularly to small businesses and local residents. However, they often face significant compliance challenges due to complex and evolving regulations. Key areas of regulatory burden include mortgage disclosure requirements, anti-money laundering (AML) obligations, and reporting mandates under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA).

The Dodd-Frank Act and subsequent regulations have introduced additional compliance requirements, which have increased the administrative and operational burdens on smaller institutions. While some regulations aim to protect consumers and promote financial stability, they can also be time-consuming and costly for community banks and credit unions to implement.

Federal regulators, including the Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC, and NCUA, have taken steps to reduce regulatory burdens through various initiatives, such as simplifying reporting requirements, providing guidance, and conducting reviews of existing regulations. The Economic Growth, Regulatory Paperwork, and Enforcement Act (EGRPRA) has been a key mechanism for identifying and addressing burdensome regulations. However, the report notes that there are still gaps in the regulatory framework, particularly with regard to the role of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) in the EGRPRA process.

The report also highlights the importance of ongoing dialogue between regulators and the financial industry to ensure that regulations are both effective and practical for smaller institutions. It recommends that the CFPB and other regulatory agencies continue to assess the impact of their rules and make necessary adjustments to reduce compliance burdens while maintaining consumer protections and financial stability.

Overall, the report underscores the need for a balanced approach to regulation that supports the continued growth and viability of community banks and credit unions, which are essential to the economic health of local communities.

Smaller community banks and credit unions must comply with some of the regulations, but compliance can be more challenging and costly for these institutions. GAO examined (1) the regulations community banks and credit unions viewed as most burdensome and why, and (2) efforts by depository institution regulators to reduce any regulatory burden. GAO analyzed regulations and interviewed more than 60 community banks and credit unions (selected based on asset size and financial activities), regulators, and industry associations and consumer groups. GAO also analyzed letters and transcripts commenting on regulatory burden that regulators prepared responding to the comments. Interviews and focus groups GAO conducted with representatives of over 60 community banks and credit unions indicated regulations for reporting mortgage characteristics, reviewing transactions for potentially illicit activity, and disclosing mortgage terms and costs to consumers were the most burdensome. Institution representatives said these regulations were time-consuming and costly to comply with, in part because the requirements were complex, required individual reports that had to be reviewed for accuracy, or mandated actions within specific timeframes. However, regulators and others noted that the regulations were essential to preventing lending discrimination and use of the banking system for illicit activity, and they were acting to reduce compliance burdens. Institution representatives also said that the new mortgage disclosure regulations increased compliance costs, added significant time to loan closings, and resulted in institutions absorbing costs when others, such as appraisers and inspectors, changed disclosed fees. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) issued guidance and conducted other outreach to educate institutions after issuing these regulations in 2013. But GAO found that some compliance burdens arose from misunderstanding the disclosure regulations—which in turn may have led institutions to take actions not actually required. Assessing the effectiveness of the guidance for the disclosure regulations could help mitigate the misunderstandings and thus also reduce compliance burdens. Regulators of community banks and credit unions—the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the National Credit Union Administration—conduct decennial reviews to obtain industry comments on regulatory burden. But the reviews, conducted under the Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act of 1996 (EGRPRA), had the following limitations: CFPB and the consumer financial regulations for which it is responsible were not included. Unlike executive branch agencies, the depository institution regulators are not required to analyze and report quantitative-based rationales for their responses to comments. Regulators do not assess the cumulative burden of the regulations they administer. CFPB has formed an internal group that will be tasked with reviewing regulations it administers, but the agency has not publicly announced the scope of regulations included, the timing and frequency of the reviews, and the extent to which they will be coordinated with the other federal banking and credit union regulators as part of their periodic EGRPRA reviews. Congressional intent in mandating that these regulators review their regulations was that the cumulative effect of all federal financial regulations be considered. In addition, sound practices required of other federal agencies require them to analyze and report their assessments when reviewing regulations. Documenting in plans how the depository institution regulators would address these EGRPRA limitations would better ensure that all regulations relevant to community banks and credit unions were reviewed, likely improve the analyses the regulators perform, and potentially result in additional burden reduction. CFPB should assess the effectiveness of guidance on mortgage disclosure regulations and publicly issue its plans for the scope and timing of its regulation reviews and coordinate these with the other regulators' review process. In written comments, CFPB and the four depository institution regulators generally agreed with the recommendations.

**Summary of the Report on the Clean Water Act and Water Infrastructure Funding**

The Clean Water Act (CWA), enacted in 1972, is the principal federal program for aiding municipal wastewater treatment plant construction and related eligible activities. Initially established under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972, the program was administered by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and provided federal grants to states for wastewater infrastructure projects. The program's goal was to improve water quality by reducing pollution and ensuring the safe discharge of treated wastewater into waterways.

Under the CWA, the federal share of project costs was initially set at 75%, but this was reduced to 55% in 1981 and further to 50% in 1981. By the mid-1980s, the program faced political and policy debates, with the Reagan administration advocating for a phaseout of federal grants in favor of state and local responsibility. This led to the 1987 amendments to the CWA, which introduced the Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF) program. The CWSRF replaced direct federal grants with low-interest loans, allowing states to finance wastewater infrastructure projects through a revolving loan fund. This shift aimed to promote long-term sustainability and reduce federal spending.

The CWSRF program was later expanded to include a Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) in 1996, following the passage of the Safe Drinking Water Act Amendments. These funds were designed to help communities finance both wastewater and drinking water infrastructure projects, with the goal of improving public health and environmental quality.

Over the years, the program has faced various challenges, including funding shortfalls, political debates over federal versus state responsibility, and the need to address aging infrastructure. In response to these challenges, Congress has periodically reauthorized and expanded the programs, including the introduction of the Water Infrastructure Financing and Investment Act (WIFIA) in 2014, which provided additional funding for large-scale water infrastructure projects.

The report highlights the importance of federal support in addressing the nation's water infrastructure needs, particularly in underserved and economically disadvantaged communities. It also underscores the ongoing need for investment in water infrastructure to meet growing demand, address climate change impacts, and ensure the long-term sustainability of water systems. The report concludes that while the federal role has evolved over time, the Clean Water Act and its associated programs remain critical to protecting public health and the environment.

In 1996, Congress amended the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA, P.L. 104-182) to authorize a similar state loan program for drinking water to help systems finance projects needed to comply with drinking water regulations and to protect public health. Since FY1997, appropriations for the drinking water state revolving loan fund (DWSRF) program have totaled $23 billion. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administers both SRF programs, which annually distribute funds to the states for implementation. Funding amounts are specified in the State and Tribal Assistance Grants (STAG) account of EPA annual appropriations acts. The combined appropriations for wastewater and drinking water infrastructure assistance have represented 25%-32% of total funds appropriated to EPA in recent years. Prior to CWA amendments in 1987 (P.L. 100-4), Congress provided wastewater grant funding directly to municipalities. The federal share of project costs was generally 55%; state and local governments were responsible for the remaining 45%. The 1987 amendments replaced this grant program with the SRF program. Local communities are now often responsible for 100% of project costs, rather than 45%, as they are required to repay loans to states. The greater financial burden of the act's loan program on some cities has caused some to seek continued grant funding. Although the CWSRF and DWSRF have largely functioned as loan programs, both allow the implementing state agency to provide "additional subsidization" under certain conditions. Since its amendments in 1996, the SDWA has authorized states to use up to 30% of their DWSRF capitalization grants to provide additional assistance, such as forgiveness of loan principal or negative interest rate loans, to help disadvantaged communities. America's Water Infrastructure Act of 2018 (AWIA; P.L. 115-270) increased this proportion to 35% while conditionally requiring states to use at least 6% of their capitalization grants for these purposes. Congress amended the CWA in 2014, adding similar provisions to the CWSRF program. In addition, appropriations acts in recent years have required states to use minimum percentages of their allotted SRF grants to provide additional subsidization. Final full-year appropriations were enacted as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, FY2019 (P.L. 116-6), on February 15, 2019. The act provided $1.694 billion for the CWSRF and $1.163 billion for the DWSRF program, nearly identical to the FY2018 appropriations. The FY0219 act provided $68 million for the WIFIA program, a $5 million increase from the FY2018 appropriation. Compared to the FY2019 appropriation levels, the Trump Administration's FY2020 budget request proposes to decrease the appropriations for the CWSRF, DWSRF, and WIFIA programs by 34%, 26%, and 63%, respectively.

This report examines the extent to which gender influences pricing in consumer goods and services, focusing on personal care products and other markets. It finds that, in many cases, products targeted to women are priced higher than those targeted to men, even when controlling for factors such as product size, brand, and promotional activity. For example, in 5 out of 10 personal care product categories analyzed, women’s versions sold at a statistically significant higher average price than men’s versions. However, the report acknowledges that these price differences may not be solely due to gender bias but could also reflect differences in consumer preferences, manufacturing costs, or market strategies.

The report also explores the broader implications of gender-based pricing in other markets, such as credit and auto services. While some studies suggest that women may face higher interest rates or less access to credit, the findings are inconsistent and often limited by data constraints. The report highlights that the conditions necessary for firms to implement price differentiation—such as market power and consumer segmentation—are present in the personal care industry, but the extent to which these practices are discriminatory remains unclear.

Federal agencies, including the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection (BCFP), the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), have the authority to investigate and address potential gender-based pricing discrimination. However, the report notes that few consumer complaints have been filed related to this issue, and agencies have not developed specific educational resources on gender-related price differences. 

Additionally, the report identifies state and local laws, such as California’s Gender Tax Repeal Act and Miami-Dade County’s Gender Pricing Ordinance, that prohibit businesses from charging different prices based on gender. These laws aim to promote price transparency and prevent discriminatory pricing practices. Despite these efforts, challenges remain in tracking and addressing gender-based price differences due to limited consumer awareness and reporting.

Overall, the report underscores the complexity of gender-based pricing and the need for further research, consumer education, and regulatory oversight to ensure fair and equitable pricing practices across all markets.
answers: Gender-related price differences occur when consumers are charged different prices for the same or similar goods and services because of factors related to gender. While variation in costs and consumer demand may give rise to such price differences, some policymakers have raised concerns that gender bias may also be a factor. While the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Fair Housing Act prohibit discrimination based on sex in credit and housing transactions, no federal law prohibits businesses from charging consumers different prices for the same or similar goods targeted to different genders. GAO was asked to review gender-related price differences for consumer goods and services sold in the United States. This report examines, among other things, (1) how prices compared for selected goods and services marketed to men and women, and potential reasons for any price differences; (2) what is known about price differences for men and women for products not differentiated by gender, such as mortgages; and (3) the extent to which federal agencies have identified and addressed any concerns about gender-related price differences. To examine these issues, GAO analyzed retail price data, reviewed relevant academic studies, analyzed federal consumer complaint data, and interviewed federal agency officials, industry experts, and academics. Firms differentiate many consumer products to appeal separately to men and women by slightly altering product attributes like color or scent. Products differentiated by gender may sell for different prices if men and women have different demands or willingness to pay for these product attributes. Of 10 personal care product categories (e.g., deodorants and shaving products) that GAO analyzed, average retail prices paid were significantly higher for women's products than for men's in 5 categories. In 2 categories—shaving gel and nondisposable razors—men's versions sold at a significantly higher price. One category—razor blades--had mixed results based on two price measures analyzed, and two others—disposable razors and mass-market perfumes—showed no significant gender price differences. GAO found that the target gender for a product is a significant factor contributing to price differences identified, but GAO did not have sufficient information to determine the extent to which these gender-related price differences were due to gender bias as opposed to other factors, such as different advertising costs. Though the analysis controlled for several observable product attributes, such as product size and packaging type, all underlying differences in costs and demand for products targeted to different genders could not be fully observed. Studies GAO reviewed found limited evidence of gender price differences for four products or services not differentiated by gender—mortgages, small business credit, auto purchases, and auto repairs. For example, with regard to mortgages, women as a group paid higher average mortgage rates than men, in part due to weaker credit characteristics, such as lower average income. However, after controlling for borrower credit characteristics and other factors, three studies did not find statistically significant differences in borrowing costs between men and women, while one found women paid higher rates for certain subprime loans. In addition, one study found that female borrowers defaulted less frequently than male borrowers with similar credit characteristics, and the study suggested that women may pay higher mortgage rates than men relative to their default risk. While these studies controlled for factors other than gender that could affect borrowing costs, several lacked important data on certain borrower risk characteristics, such as credit scores, which could affect analysis of gender disparities. Also, several studies analyzed small samples of subprime loans that were originated in 2005 or earlier, which limits the generalizability of the results. In their oversight of federal antidiscrimination statutes, the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, Federal Trade Commission, and Department of Housing and Urban Development have identified limited consumer concerns based on gender-related pricing differences. GAO's analysis of complaint data received by the three agencies from 2012–2017 found that they had received limited consumer complaints about gender-related price differences. The agencies provide general consumer education resources on discrimination and consumer awareness. However, given the limited consumer concern, they have not identified a need to incorporate additional materials specific to gender-related price differences into their existing consumer education resources.

The U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) oversees the safety of approximately 1,000 non-federal hydropower projects, which include over 2,500 dams. These dams contribute about 8% of the nation’s total electric generating capacity. FERC’s role is to license and regulate these projects to ensure safe operation, with licensees responsible for maintaining and repairing dams using sound engineering practices. FERC employs a multi-layered safety oversight approach that includes regular inspections, engineering studies, and relicensing processes.

FERC conducts safety inspections of dams, which are guided by its Operating Manual and Engineering Guidelines. These inspections involve reviewing documents, conducting field assessments, and identifying safety deficiencies. FERC staff generally follow these procedures, but the agency faces challenges in consistently recording and analyzing inspection data across its five regional offices. Different systems, such as DAMS and OEP-IT, are used to track safety information, leading to inconsistencies that limit the usefulness of the data for broader risk analysis.

To improve safety oversight, FERC is working on replacing some of its systems and standardizing how safety information is recorded. Additionally, FERC uses engineering studies—such as hydrology, seismicity, and stability analyses—to evaluate dam performance. These studies are reviewed by FERC staff and consultants, with the frequency and depth of review depending on the dam’s hazard classification. While FERC has made progress in ensuring dam safety through inspections and relicensing, it has not yet conducted a comprehensive portfolio-wide analysis of safety risks across all its regulated dams.

The report highlights the need for FERC to enhance its ability to analyze safety risks at a national level, similar to how it responded to the Oroville Dam incident. This would allow FERC to identify common safety deficiencies and prioritize remediation efforts. The report also recommends that FERC develop standard procedures for recording inspection findings and improve its data management systems to support more effective risk analysis and oversight. Overall, FERC’s current approach to dam safety is robust, but improvements in data consistency and portfolio-wide risk analysis could further strengthen its regulatory effectiveness.

The factors that contributed to Puerto Rico's financial condition and levels of debt relate to (1) the Puerto Rico government running persistent annual deficits—where expenses exceed revenues—and (2) its use of debt to cope with deficits. Based on a literature review and interviews with current and former Puerto Rico officials, federal officials, and other relevant experts, GAO identified factors that contributed to Puerto Rico's persistent deficits: The Puerto Rico government's inadequate financial management and oversight practices. For example, the Puerto Rico government frequently overestimated the amount of revenue it would collect and Puerto Rico's agencies regularly spent more than the amounts Puerto Rico's legislature appropriated for a given fiscal year. Policy decisions by Puerto Rico's government. For example, Puerto Rico borrowed funds to balance budgets and insufficiently addressed public pension funding shortfalls. Puerto Rico's prolonged economic contraction. Examples of factors contributing to the contraction include outmigration and the resulting diminished labor force, and the high cost of importing goods and energy. Additional factors enabled Puerto Rico to use debt to finance its deficits, such as high demand for Puerto Rico debt. One cause of high demand was that under federal law, income from Puerto Rico bonds generally receives more favorable tax treatment than income from bonds issued by states and their localities. Based on an assessment of relevant literature and input from current and former Puerto Rico officials, federal officials, and other relevant experts, GAO identified three potential federal actions that may help address some of these factors. However, reduced demand could hinder Puerto Rico's ability to borrow funds for capital investments or liquidity. Apply federal investor protection laws to Puerto Rico. Requiring Puerto Rico investment companies to disclose risks with Puerto Rico bonds and adhere to other requirements could lower demand for the bonds. However, this action could also limit Puerto Rico's ability to borrow funds. Modify the Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) authority over municipal bond disclosure requirements. SEC could be allowed to require timely disclosure of materials—such as audited financial statements—associated with municipal bonds. Timely disclosure could help investors make informed decisions about investing in municipal bonds. However, a broad requirement could place additional burdens on all U.S. municipal issuers, such as the costs of standardizing reporting.

These programs collectively serve millions of Americans and are among the largest and most complex in the U.S. federal government. Medicare and Medicaid, in particular, have seen significant growth in spending and enrollment, with Medicare projected to reach $1.3 trillion in 2026 and Medicaid expected to exceed $950 billion by 2025. Both programs have increasingly adopted managed-care delivery systems, with a growing percentage of beneficiaries enrolled in managed-care plans.

Fraud, waste, and abuse remain critical concerns for CMS, with improper payments estimated at over $75 billion annually. To combat these issues, CMS has established several antifraud initiatives, including the Health Care Fraud and Abuse Control (HCFAC) program and the Medicaid Integrity Program. These programs receive substantial funding and support a range of activities, including audits, investigations, and provider education. The Center for Program Integrity (CPI) serves as the focal point for CMS’s antifraud efforts, working across Medicare and Medicaid to address fraud risks through a spectrum of activities, from correcting unintentional errors to investigating serious fraudulent schemes.

CMS has also implemented various control measures, such as the Fraud Prevention System (FPS), which uses predictive analytics to identify potential fraud, and the Unified Program Integrity Contractors (UPIC), which help detect and investigate fraudulent activities. The agency has made strides in improving coordination and communication across its programs, reorganizing its structure to better address cross-cutting vulnerabilities and enhance collaboration with stakeholders.

Despite these efforts, CMS has not yet conducted a comprehensive fraud risk assessment for Medicare and Medicaid, which is a key component of the Fraud Risk Framework. Such an assessment would help the agency develop a risk-based antifraud strategy, prioritize resources, and ensure that its efforts are aligned with the most significant fraud risks. The report recommends that CMS implement a structured approach to fraud risk management, including regular training for employees, the development of a fraud risk assessment, and the creation of a documented antifraud strategy.

In conclusion, while CMS has made significant progress in managing fraud risks across its programs, there is a need for a more strategic and comprehensive approach to ensure the continued protection of taxpayer funds and the integrity of these vital health programs. The recommendations provided aim to strengthen CMS’s antifraud efforts and align them with best practices in risk management.

The Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) program, authorized by Congress in 2011 and signed into law by the President, aims to modernize and preserve public housing by converting it into project-based rental assistance (PBRA) or project-based voucher (PBV) contracts. The program allows public housing authorities (PHAs) to use a variety of funding sources, including Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), to finance rehabilitation, new construction, and long-term affordability. As of September 2017, the program had reached its full capacity of 225,000 units, with over 74,000 units converted.

RAD conversions typically involve rehabilitation or new construction, with 61% of closed conversions involving planned rehabilitation. The majority of conversions used LIHTC, but the program also relied on other funding sources such as mortgages and public housing funds. The average construction cost per unit was approximately $60,000, with total construction costs reaching $4.4 billion. However, HUD’s leverage ratio, which measures the amount of private capital leveraged per public dollar, was found to be inconsistent and potentially overstated due to methodological issues in data collection and categorization.

The report highlights several challenges in HUD’s oversight of RAD conversions, including limited post-conversion monitoring, inconsistent data collection, and inadequate tracking of resident impacts. While RAD conversions have improved living conditions for many residents, concerns were raised about the adequacy of resident protections, the effectiveness of relocation processes, and the long-term affordability of converted properties. Additionally, HUD’s procedures for ensuring that converted properties remain affordable in the event of default, bankruptcy, or foreclosure were found to be insufficient.

The report also notes that HUD has not fully developed monitoring procedures for certain resident safeguards, such as the right to relocation and choice mobility, and has not yet implemented comprehensive post-conversion oversight. The findings suggest that HUD needs to improve its data collection, enhance its monitoring capabilities, and ensure that all RAD provisions are effectively implemented to protect residents and maintain the long-term affordability of public housing.

In conclusion, while the RAD program has made significant strides in modernizing public housing and improving living conditions, there are critical areas where HUD needs to strengthen its oversight and data collection to ensure the program’s long-term success and compliance with its statutory goals. The recommendations provided in the report aim to address these gaps and improve the effectiveness of the RAD program.

RAD allows PHAs to move (convert) properties in the public housing program to Section 8 rental assistance programs, and retain property ownership or transfer it to other entities. The conversion enables PHAs to access additional funding, including investor equity, generally not available for public housing properties. This report addresses, among other objectives, HUD's (1) assessment of conversion outcomes; (2) oversight of resident safeguards; and (3) provisions to help preserve the long-term affordability of units. GAO analyzed data on RAD conversions through fiscal year 2017; reviewed a sample of randomly selected, nongeneralizable RAD property files; and interviewed HUD officials, PHAs, developers, academics, and affected residents. RAD's authorizing legislation requires HUD to assess and publish findings about the amount of private-sector leveraging. HUD uses a variety of metrics to measure conversion outcomes. But, the metric HUD uses to measure private-sector leveraging—the share of private versus public funding for construction or rehabilitation of assisted housing—has limitations. For example, HUD's leveraging ratio counts some public resources as leveraged private-sector investment and does not use final (post-completion) data. As a result, HUD's ability to accurately assess private-sector leveraging is limited. HUD does not systematically use its data systems to track effects of RAD conversions on resident households (such as changes in rent and income, or relocation) or monitor use of all resident safeguards. Rather, since 2016, HUD has required public housing agencies (PHA) or other post-conversion owners to maintain resident logs and collect such information. But the resident logs do not contain historical program information. HUD has not developed a process for systematically reviewing information from its data systems and resident logs on an ongoing basis. HUD has been developing procedures to monitor compliance with some resident safeguards—such as the right to return to a converted property—and begun a limited review of compliance with these safeguards. However, HUD has not yet developed a process for monitoring other safeguards—such as access to other housing voucher options. Federal internal control standards require agencies to use quality information to achieve objectives, and obtain and evaluate relevant and reliable data in a timely manner for use in effective monitoring. Without a comprehensive review of household information and procedures for fully monitoring all resident safeguards, HUD cannot fully assess the effects of RAD on residents. RAD authorizing legislation and the program's use agreements (contracts with property owners) contain provisions intended to help ensure the long-term availability of affordable units, but the provisions have not been tested in situations such as foreclosure. For example, use agreements between HUD and property owners specify affordability and use restrictions that according to the contract would survive a default or foreclosure. HUD officials stated that HUD intends to develop procedures to identify and respond to risks to long-term affordability, including default or foreclosure in RAD properties. However, HUD has not yet done so. According to federal internal control standards, agencies should identify, analyze, and respond to risks related to achieving goals and objectives. Procedures that address oversight of affordability requirements would better position HUD to help ensure RAD conversions comply with program requirements, detect potential foreclosure and other risks, and take corrective actions. GAO makes five recommendations to HUD intended to improve leveraging metrics, monitoring of the use and enforcement of resident safeguards, and compliance with RAD requirements. HUD agreed with our recommendations to improve metrics and build on existing oversight.

The U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) has experienced a decline in the size of its military, civilian, and contractor workforce since peaking around 2011. This change has been influenced by factors such as reduced U.S. involvement in conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, shifts in workforce composition, and the growth of specialized areas like acquisition and cyber. DOD manages its workforce under several statutes, including Title 10 of the United States Code, which outlines policies for determining the most cost-effective mix of military, civilian, and contracted services.

DOD Instruction 1100.22 provides a framework for determining the appropriate workforce mix, emphasizing cost comparisons for new or expanding mission requirements. In 2013, DOD improved its methodology for estimating the full cost of work performed by military and civilian personnel and contractors, though limitations remained, particularly in accounting for overhead and non-labor costs. DOD implemented some recommendations but not all, and the methodology used in the Cost-Comparison Report partially addressed the mandate to account for the full cost of civilian and contractor personnel.

The report highlights that DOD compared the costs of similar functions performed by civilians and contractors at selected installations, such as Fort Belvoir Community Hospital and Naval Medical Center San Diego. However, the results were not generalizable across the department, and non-labor costs were excluded from the analysis. DOD officials noted that the methodology was in line with DODI 7041.04, which allows for the exclusion of common costs when personnel numbers are equivalent. Nevertheless, the report acknowledges that in many cases, personnel numbers differed, and thus, the exclusion of non-labor costs may have skewed the comparison.

DOD also assessed flexible employment authorities for civilian hiring, identifying variations in their use and suggesting potential improvements. While DOD partially addressed the mandated reporting elements, it did not fully account for the full cost of personnel, as required by the congressional mandate. The report concludes that DOD needs to refine its cost estimation methods and ensure that all relevant costs are included in future analyses to better inform workforce management decisions. The findings are part of a broader effort to improve the accuracy and comprehensiveness of DOD’s workforce data, supporting more effective leadership and resource allocation.

**Summary of the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) Report**

The Federal Housing Administration (FHA), established in 1934 under the National Housing Act, is a government agency within the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that provides mortgage insurance to private lenders. This insurance protects lenders against the risk of borrower default, ensuring they are repaid the remaining balance of the loan if a borrower fails to meet their obligations. Unlike the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), FHA does not restrict mortgage eligibility based on veteran status, income, or property location, making it the most broadly targeted of the three federal mortgage insurance programs.

FHA-insured mortgages are designed to increase access to affordable home ownership, particularly for first-time buyers, low- and moderate-income households, and minority communities. These loans typically require lower down payments—starting at 3.5% for borrowers with a credit score of 580 or higher—and have more lenient credit requirements compared to conventional mortgages. This report evaluates the alignment of selected federal agencies' physical security assessment methodologies with the Interagency Security Committee (ISC) Risk Management Process for Federal Facilities. The ISC, established in 1995 following the Oklahoma City bombing, is tasked with developing and enforcing security standards to protect federal facilities. The report highlights that while the ISC Standard outlines a comprehensive risk management process, many agencies have not fully implemented methodologies that adhere to these standards.

The report focuses on four agencies: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), and the U.S. Forest Service. It finds that none of these agencies’ methodologies fully align with the ISC Standard, which requires assessing all 33 undesirable events and evaluating threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences for each. Instead, agencies often rely on outdated checklists or standardized approaches that fail to account for facility-specific risks.

Key issues identified include inconsistent application of risk assessment methodologies, lack of documentation for deviations from baseline countermeasures, and failure to reassess facilities within the required 3-year interval. These shortcomings hinder agencies’ ability to make informed decisions about resource allocation and security measures, potentially leading to either under- or over-protection of facilities.

The report also highlights challenges in managing the assessment backlog, insufficient staffing, and competing priorities that delay the implementation of updated policies and procedures. Without proper risk assessments, agencies may not be able to justify the need for costly security measures or reallocate resources effectively.

To address these issues, the report recommends that agencies update their policies and procedures to align with the ISC Standard, implement a comprehensive risk assessment framework, and ensure ongoing monitoring of security programs. It also calls for improved data collection and analysis to support informed decision-making and effective resource management.

Overall, the findings underscore the importance of adhering to the ISC Risk Management Process to ensure the security of federal facilities and the protection of personnel and assets. The agencies’ ability to meet these standards will be critical in maintaining the safety and operational effectiveness of their facilities.

None of the four agencies GAO reviewed—U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the Agricultural Research Service (ARS), and the Forest Service—used security assessment methodologies that fully aligned with the Interagency Security Committee's Risk Management Process for Federal Facilities standard (the ISC Standard). This standard requires that methodologies used to identify necessary facility countermeasures—such as fences and closed-circuit televisions—must: 1. Consider all of the undesirable events (i.e., arson and vandalism) identified by the ISC Standard as possible risks to facilities. 2. Assess three factors—threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences—for each of these events and use these three factors to measure risk. All four agencies used methodologies that included some ISC requirements when conducting assessments. CBP and FAA assessed vulnerabilities but not threats and consequences. ARS and the Forest Service assessed threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences, but did not use these factors to measure risk. In addition, the agencies considered many, but not all 33 undesirable events related to physical security as possible risks to their facilities. Agencies are taking steps to improve their methodologies. For example, ARS and the Forest Service now use a methodology that measures risk and plan to incorporate the methodology into policy. Although CBP and FAA have updated their methodologies, their policies do not require methodologies that fully align with the ISC standard. As a result, these agencies miss the opportunity for a more informed assessment of the risk to their facilities. All four agencies reported facing management challenges in conducting physical security assessments or monitoring assessment results. FAA does not routinely monitor the performance of its physical security program. answers: Congress has delegated responsibility for monetary policy to the Federal Reserve (the Fed), the nation's central bank, but retains oversight responsibilities for ensuring that the Fed is adhering to its statutory mandate of "maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates." To meet its price stability mandate, the Fed has set a longer-run goal of 2% inflation. The Fed's control over monetary policy stems from its exclusive ability to alter the money supply and credit conditions more broadly. Normally, the Fed conducts monetary policy by setting a target for the federal funds rate, the rate at which banks borrow and lend reserves on an overnight basis. It meets its target through open market operations, financial transactions traditionally involving U.S. Treasury securities. Beginning in 2007, the federal funds target was reduced from 5.25% to a range of 0% to 0.25% in December 2008, which economists call the zero lower bound. By historical standards, rates were kept unusually low for an unusually long time to mitigate the effects of the financial crisis and its aftermath. Starting in December 2015, the Fed has been raising interest rates and expects to gradually raise rates further. The Fed raised rates once in 2016, three times in 2017, and four times in 2018, by 0.25 percentage points each time. In light of increased economic uncertainty and financial volatility, the Fed announced in January 2019 that it would be "patient" before raising rates again. The Fed influences interest rates to affect interest-sensitive spending, such as business capital spending on plant and equipment, household spending on consumer durables, and residential investment. In addition, when interest rates diverge between countries, it causes capital flows that affect the exchange rate between foreign currencies and the dollar, which in turn affects spending on exports and imports. Through these channels, monetary policy can be used to stimulate or slow aggregate spending in the short run. In the long run, monetary policy mainly affects inflation. A low and stable rate of inflation promotes price transparency and, thereby, sounder economic decisions. The Fed's relative independence from Congress and the Administration has been justified by many economists on the grounds that it reduces political pressure to make monetary policy decisions that are inconsistent with a long-term focus on stable inflation. But independence reduces accountability to Congress and the Administration, and recent legislation and criticism of the Fed by the President has raised the question about the proper balance between the two. While the federal funds target was at the zero lower bound, the Fed attempted to provide additional stimulus through unsterilized purchases of Treasury and mortgage-backed securities (MBS), a practice popularly referred to as quantitative easing (QE). Between 2009 and 2014, the Fed undertook three rounds of QE. The third round was completed in October 2014, at which point the Fed's balance sheet was $4.5 trillion—five times its precrisis size. After QE ended, the Fed maintained the balance sheet at the same level until September 2017, when it began to very gradually reduce it to a more normal size. The Fed has raised interest rates in the presence of a large balance sheet through the use of two new tools—by paying banks interest on reserves held at the Fed and by engaging in reverse repurchase agreements (reverse repos) through a new overnight facility. In January 2019, the Fed announced that it would continue using these tools to set interest rates permanently, in which case the balance sheet may not get much smaller than its current size of $4 trillion. With regard to its mandate, the Fed believes that unemployment is currently lower than the rate that it considers consistent with maximum employment, and inflation is close to the Fed's 2% goal by the Fed's preferred measure. Even after recent rate increases, monetary policy is still considered expansionary. This monetary policy stance is unusually stimulative compared with policy in this stage of previous expansions, and is being coupled with a stimulative fiscal policy (larger structural budget deficit). Debate is currently focused on how quickly the Fed should raise rates. Some contend the greater risk is that raising rates too slowly at full employment will cause inflation to become too high or cause financial instability, whereas others contend that raising rates too quickly will cause inflation to remain too low and choke off the expansion.

The Buy American Act of 1933 was established during the Great Depression to promote domestic job creation by giving the federal government a preference for purchasing end products made in the United States. The Act applies to most federal procurements, with exceptions for products valued below the micro-purchase threshold ($3,500 in fiscal year 2017) and those intended for use outside the U.S. However, the Act also includes several exceptions and waivers that allow federal agencies to procure foreign end products under specific conditions.

Key exceptions include the domestic non-availability exception, the unreasonable cost exception, and the Trade Agreements Act (TAA) waivers, which apply to purchases from countries with which the U.S. has trade agreements. The TAA allows for nondiscriminatory treatment of foreign products from designated countries, provided the procurement meets certain value thresholds. Additionally, the Department of Defense (DOD) has a public interest exception that permits procurement from 27 qualifying countries without regard to trade agreement thresholds.

The report highlights that in fiscal year 2017, the federal government obligated approximately $7.8 billion for foreign end products, representing less than 5% of total federal contract obligations. However, data collection and reporting through the Federal Procurement Data System-Next Generation (FPDS-NG) are inconsistent and error-prone, with inaccuracies in reporting the use of exceptions and waivers. The system lacks features to prevent misreporting, and some agencies do not provide sufficient guidance or training to contracting officers on how to apply the Buy American Act requirements.

The report also notes that while DOD has implemented comprehensive training and guidance, other agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) have varying levels of support and training for their contracting officers. This lack of uniformity can lead to confusion and errors in procurement decisions.

The report concludes with recommendations for improving the accuracy of data reporting, enhancing training and guidance for contracting officers, and clarifying the applicability of exceptions and waivers under the Buy American Act. These improvements are essential to ensure compliance with the Act and to support informed procurement decisions that align with national economic and security interests.

RRA is financed primarily by payroll taxes, financial interchanges from Social Security, and transfers from the National Railroad Retirement Investment Trust (NRRIT). Railroad retirement payroll taxes have two tiers: the Tier I tax is essentially the same as the Social Security payroll tax and the Tier II tax is set each year based on the railroad retirement system's asset balances, benefit payments, and administrative costs. Tier I annuities are designed to be nearly equivalent to Social Security benefits and are based on both railroad retirement and Social Security-covered employment. However, Tier I annuities are more generous than Social Security benefits in certain situations. For example, at the age of 60, railroad workers with at least 30 years of covered railroad work may receive unreduced retirement annuities. Tier II annuities are similar to private pensions and based solely on covered railroad service. Tier II annuities are paid in addition to Tier I annuities. Railroad disability annuities may be payable to totally disabled railroad workers who are permanently disabled from all work and occupational disabled workers who are found to be permanently disabled from their regular railroad occupations. Eligible spouses and survivors of railroad workers may receive a certain portion of Tier I and Tier II benefits, but divorced spouses and surviving divorced spouses are eligible for only a certain portion of Tier I benefits. The Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act (RUIA) authorizes unemployment and sickness benefits for railroad workers. RUIA is financed solely by railroad employers, whose contributions are based on the taxable earnings of their employees. Eligibility for railroad unemployment and sickness benefits is based on recent railroad service and earnings. The maximum daily unemployment and sickness benefit payable in the benefit year that began July 1, 2018, is $77, and the maximum benefit for a biweekly claim is $770. Normal benefits are paid for up to 26 weeks in a benefit year. The railroad unemployment and sickness system remains affected by sequestration, as unemployment benefits will continue to be reduced through at least September 30, 2019.
